title: Stack and Heap Concepts
learningObjectives: Explain the core execution or memory concept in this lesson.
Identify how state, data, or execution contexts are involved.
Trace a small example and record relevant changes.
Recognize a misconception and correct it.
Apply the concept to a simple scenario.

understand.concept: Stack and heap are common conceptual memory models. The stack often tracks active function calls and local execution contexts. The heap often contains dynamically managed objects or data whose lifetime is not simply tied to one call. Implementation and optimization vary by language and runtime, so these are models rather than universal placement rules.
understand.whyItMatters: Understanding these models prepares learners to reason about function calls, recursion depth, object lifetime, and memory/resource management without assuming exact runtime layout.
understand.analogy: Temporary work trays and a shared storage area can illustrate active call contexts versus dynamically managed data. Real runtimes can optimize or move data, so it is not literal.
understand.analogyLimit: This is a simplified model; actual behavior and implementation vary by language and environment.

explain.narrative: Trace the program carefully: record the initial values, follow each instruction, and update your state notes. Distinguish names from values and references. Where memory is discussed, avoid claiming exact physical placement from source code alone.

examples.title: Function call
examples.explanation: The runtime tracks an active function call; stack memory is not directly shown.

examples.title: Nested calls
examples.explanation: The inner call returns before the outer call finishes in synchronous execution.

examples.title: Object returned
examples.explanation: The object remains reachable after the function returns; storage is runtime-managed.

examples.title: Recursive calls
examples.code:
function step(n) { if (n === 0) return 0; return step(n-1); }
console.log(step(2));
examples.explanation: Recursive calls create active contexts conceptually; very deep recursion may hit runtime limits.

examples.title: Physical placement
examples.code:
// Source code alone does not prove exact physical memory placement.
// Runtime optimizations can affect representation.
examples.explanation: Stack and heap are useful models; exact implementation details vary.

commonMistakes: Assuming variable names are physical addresses.
Assuming every assignment creates a deep copy.
Treating stack and heap models as universal placement guarantees.
Ignoring current state while tracing a condition.
Inferring exact memory layout from source code.

guidedTask.title: Guided practice: Stack and Heap Concepts
guidedTask.instructions: Trace a small program using a state table or memory sketch and explain the behavior.
steps: Record the initial values or state.
Update the state table after each relevant statement.
Draw a reference or call-context sketch where useful.
Compare your prediction with the output and explain any difference.
guidedTask.starterCode: // Write a short example and trace its state changes manually.

independentTask.title: Independent practice: execution and state trace
independentTask.instructions: Write a small example demonstrating the topic and explain its execution.
requirements: Show at least three operations or observations.
Include a function call or reference if relevant.
Test a second input or state.
Explain which implementation details are conceptual, not guaranteed.

hints: For objects, check whether names share a reference.
Trace nested calls in execution order.
Treat memory diagrams as conceptual models.

questions.prompt: What is a useful way to understand a running program?
options: Trace instructions and the state they read or change
questions.answer: Trace instructions and the state they read or change
questions.explanation: Execution is a sequence of operations that may observe or change state.

questions.prompt: What does a state transition represent?
options: A change from one state to another due to an operation or event
A comment in the source file
questions.answer: A change from one state to another due to an operation or event
questions.explanation: Transitions describe state changes and may have conditions.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes value and address?
options: A value is data; an address identifies a storage location where address concepts are exposed
Every variable name is an address
Values and addresses are always identical
questions.answer: A value is data; an address identifies a storage location where address concepts are exposed
questions.explanation: Names, values, and storage locations are distinct concepts.

questions.prompt: Which statement about stack and heap models is accurate?
options: They are useful concepts, but implementation varies by language and runtime
Every value always resides on the stack
The heap is never managed by a runtime
questions.answer: They are useful concepts, but implementation varies by language and runtime
questions.explanation: Stack and heap are common models, not universal physical placement guarantees.

questions.prompt: What should you avoid claiming from source code alone?
options: The exact physical address or placement of every value
The declared name of a variable
The output of a simple expression
questions.answer: The exact physical address or placement of every value
questions.explanation: Runtime representation and optimizations mean source code alone rarely proves exact placement.
